title: Transactions under concurrency
summary: Make a read-modify-write transfer atomic and lock the rows it depends on.

scenario.briefing: Two cashiers can transfer from the same account at the same time. The current code reads a balance, checks it, and writes a new value, so one transfer can overwrite the other.

objectives.description: Apply the taught syntax in a working file.
Review an artifact and identify the concrete risks.

hints: BEGIN starts the unit; COMMIT makes it durable; ROLLBACK discards it.
A plain SELECT does not lock the row. Add FOR UPDATE to hold it until commit.
Lock the two accounts in the same order every time to avoid deadlocks.
Guard the debit with balance_cents >= 2500 and roll back when it matches no row.

misconceptions.description: Confusing statement atomicity with transaction atomicity.
misconceptions.feedback: Each statement is atomic by itself. Two statements need an explicit transaction to succeed or fail together.

misconceptions.description: Believing READ COMMITTED prevents lost updates.
misconceptions.feedback: Two transactions can still read the same balance and write over each other. Lock the row or use an atomic conditional update.

misconceptions.description: Reading the balance first and locking afterward.
misconceptions.feedback: The value read before FOR UPDATE can already be stale. Lock first, then use the locked row.

sections.title: A transaction is one unit of work
sections.body: BEGIN starts the unit, COMMIT makes all of it durable, and ROLLBACK discards all of it. Without a transaction, a failure between the debit and the credit leaves the accounts unbalanced.

sections.title: Isolation levels do not replace locks
sections.body: READ COMMITTED gives each statement a fresh snapshot, so two transactions can read the same balance and write over each other. REPEATABLE READ holds one snapshot and can abort a conflicting write in PostgreSQL, but a read-modify-write that computes an absolute value from an old snapshot still needs a lock or an atomic update. FOR UPDATE makes the row lock explicit and works at either level.

sections.title: Lock in a stable order
sections.body: Concurrent transactions that lock the same rows in different orders can deadlock. Lock accounts in a consistent order, keep the transaction short, and check the affected row count so a failed guard aborts the work.

vocabulary.definition: A group of statements that commit or roll back together.
The visibility rules for concurrent transactions.
One transaction overwrites another transaction's committed change.
A lock that blocks other writers from changing a row until the transaction ends.
Two transactions waiting for locks the other holds.

steps.title: Transfer funds in one transaction
steps.prompt: Edit transaction.sql. Move 2500 cents from acct-a to acct-b as one atomic unit: open a transaction, lock both rows in a stable order, guard the debit, and commit. Show the rollback path for an abandoned transfer.

tests.description: The transfer opens a transaction with an explicit isolation level.
includes: SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL READ COMMITTED;

tests.description: Both account rows are locked before they are changed.
includes:
SELECT balance_cents
FROM accounts
WHERE id = 'acct-a'
FOR UPDATE;

SELECT balance_cents
FROM accounts
WHERE id = 'acct-b'
FOR UPDATE;

tests.description: The debit is guarded and the credit follows it.
The successful path commits and the abandoned path rolls back.

steps.title: Review the withdrawal path
steps.prompt: Review the artifact and select every real concurrency problem.

artifact.title: withdraw.ts
artifact.caption: Two requests can call withdraw for the same account at the same time.

findings.label: Two concurrent withdrawals can read the same balance before either writes.
The UPDATE writes an absolute balance computed from a stale read, so one withdrawal can be lost.
The read and write are not protected by a transaction or a row lock.
A single UPDATE that subtracts the amount and checks balance_cents >= $1 plus the row count would close the race.
Wrapping the same statements in a READ COMMITTED transaction is enough to prevent the lost update.

verdicts.label: Block the change until the balance update is atomic or row-locked.
Ship it; the database serializes the two updates.
Only naming and formatting need work.

steps.explanation: Both requests read the same balance, both pass the check, and both write a balance derived from that stale read. Use a conditional atomic UPDATE or lock the row with FOR UPDATE inside a transaction.
